q: Under the Formula in Sec. 4.1, at what minimum distance from the Architect's area of operation must local consultants and technical staff be assigned before transportation, per diem, and housing/living allowances become reimbursable (R)?
o: Over 100 km
Any distance outside Metro Manila
Over 50 km
Over 200 km
Over 500 km
n: The Formula defines R as including such allowances for consultants and technical staff "if assigned to places over 100 km. from the area of operation of the Architect." (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1 (Formula))

q: An Architect engaged for Pre-Design Services brings in a structural engineering firm to provide specialized input, formalized under the extended terms of the Owner-Architect Agreement. Which manner of rendering services under Sec. 3.2 does this describe?
o: Through the Architect's Own Staff (Sec. 3.2.2)
Promotional Services (Sec. 2.12)
As an individual Architect (Sec. 3.2.1)
By Association, Consultation, or Networking (Sec. 3.2.3)
n: Sec. 3.2.3 describes consultation between an Architect and a firm of other disciplines under the extended terms of the Owner-Architect Agreement as association/consultation/networking. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 3.2.3)

q: Judging from the range of services SPP Document 201 enumerates — from consultation and feasibility studies through design brief preparation — which stage of a project's life cycle does it govern overall?
o: The Pre-Design phase
The building permit phase
The construction supervision phase
The post-occupancy phase
n: Sec. 2 describes Pre-Design Services as covering services "ranging from initial problem identification to activities that would allow the Architect to initially conceptualize" solutions — i.e., the stage preceding actual design. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2)

q: Under what situation is Professional Fee Plus Expenses (Sec. 4.2) most commonly used, and what must first be agreed upon to keep the fee equitable?
o: No scope agreement, only a deadline
For a series of projects; scope agreed first
Only for government contracts
Only for one-time residential jobs
n: Sec. 4.2 states this method is frequently used where there is a continuing relationship involving a series of projects, establishing a fixed sum above reimbursement for technical time and overhead, requiring agreement on the general scope of work. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.2)

q: As part of the IRR of which law is SPP Document 201 described as having been issued?
o: P.D. 1096 (National Building Code)
R.A. No. 386 (Civil Code)
n: The document header states SPP Doc. 201 on Pre-Design Services is "Part of the IRR of R.A. No. 9266," the Architecture Act. (Source: SPP Document 201, Title/Header)

q: Which description best fits Architectural Programming (Sec. 2.7)?
o: A cost-based accounting exercise
A problem-seeking analysis yielding a space program
The drafting of construction schedules
The signing and sealing of plans
n: Sec. 2.7 describes Architectural Programming as an analytical problem-seeking process identifying horizontal and vertical requirements and incorporating a space program with characterizations like ambiance and cost range. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.7)

q: A Client asks the Architect, acting purely as agent, to inspect a possible project site and attend an out-of-town investment meeting on the Client's behalf. Per Sec. 4.4, how may the Architect be paid for this personal-time work?
o: Per diem and honorarium, plus expenses
One lump sum fixed at the start
Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense only
No compensation may be accepted
n: Sec. 4.4 covers activities like project-related meetings/trips, ocular site inspections, and conferring on prospective investments, compensable on a per diem and honorarium basis plus out-of-pocket expenses (travel, accommodations, subsistence). (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.4)

q: Which of these is NOT part of the Scope of Pre-Design Services listed in SPP Doc. 201, Sec. 2?
o: Value management
Construction supervision
Feasibility studies
Architectural programming
n: Sec. 2 lists consultation, pre-feasibility and feasibility studies, site selection/analysis, site utilization and land-use studies, architectural research, architectural programming, space planning, space management studies, value management, design brief preparation, and promotional services — construction supervision is a separate SPP document, not a Pre-Design service. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2)

q: How many manners of rendering Pre-Design services does SPP Doc. 201, Sec. 3.2 recognize, and what are they?
o: One: through his own staff only
Three: individual, own staff, or association
Two: individual or government employee
Four, including foreign outsourcing
n: Sec. 3.2 lists three manners: (3.2.1) as an individual Architect, (3.2.2) through the Architect's own staff, and (3.2.3) by association, consultation, or networking. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 3.2)

q: Given the number of report sets the Client actually asked for, how many of those sets qualify as a billable extra reimbursable cost item under the Formula's definition of R?
o: 5 sets
8 sets
3 sets
0 sets
n: R includes the "cost of printing of extra set of drawings, reports, maps, contract documents, etc. over the five (5) copies submitted to the Client." Since 5 copies are standard, 8 - 5 = 3 extra sets are billable as reimbursable cost. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1 (Formula, definition of R))
scenario: A Client engages an Architect to carry out a feasibility study as a Pre-Design Service, compensated under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method. Time logs show the Architect himself put in 40 hours at ₱800/hour, a Consultant contributed 20 hours at ₱1,000/hour, and the Technical Staff logged 60 hours at ₱300/hour. To cover overhead and profit, the firm applies a multiplier of 2.0. Since the project site sits 150 km from the Architect's area of operation, the Consultant and Technical Staff ran up reimbursable travel and lodging costs totaling ₱15,000. On top of that, the Client asked for 8 sets of the feasibility report, more than the standard number of copies ordinarily submitted to the Client.

q: Per the Introduction of SPP Doc. 201, why must the Architect keep expanding basic services over time even though those services have stayed largely the same?
o: The Board mandates new services every 5 years
UAP dues fund new service categories
Rising client demands, standards, technology, laws
Foreign architects are limited to them
n: Sec. 1.1 states the Architect must expand services in response to increasing Client demands, evolving standards of regulated professional practice, advancing technology, and new laws. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 1.1)

q: An Architect meets a prospective Client, gives written advice on a contemplated project, but the Client ultimately drops the idea. How should SPP Doc. 201 characterize this engagement?
o: As an invalid engagement, since no fee attaches unless the project proceeds
As Consultation — a valid Pre-Design service regardless of the project's eventual outcome
As a violation of the Code of Ethics
As Architectural Research only
n: Consultation (Sec. 2.1) covers oral/written advice, conferences, and evaluations, and is a valid, compensable Pre-Design service whether or not the Client pursues the project. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.1)

q: The Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method (Sec. 4.1) applies only to which kind of work, and for what reason?
o: Non-creative work; hours can't value design
Work by foreign consultants only
Purely creative design work
Construction supervision only
n: Sec. 4.1 states this cost-based method applies only to non-creative work (accounting, secretarial, research, data gathering, report preparation) since creative design's value cannot be measured by time spent. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1)

q: In terms of data requirements, how do Feasibility Studies (Sec. 2.3) differ from Pre-Feasibility Studies?
o: Both rely only on secondary data
Feasibility adds primary data; pre-feasibility is secondary
Feasibility secondary; pre-feasibility primary
Feasibility ignores present and future trends
n: Sec. 2.3 states Feasibility Studies involve detailed analysis based on the pre-feasibility studies and require primary data gathering and analysis to determine viability and forecast performance over time. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.3)

q: Per Sec. 3.1, once the initial meeting/conversation/correspondence with the Client concludes, what must the Architect submit before rendering Pre-Design Services, and what should it cover?
o: A proposal on scope, payment, owner's duties, conditions
A verbal confirmation of the fee
A notarized deed of sale for the lot
A signed as-built survey of the site
n: Sec. 3.1 requires the Architect to submit a proposal for pre-design services stating the Scope of Work (3.1.1), Manner of Payment (3.1.2), Owner's Responsibilities, and Other Conditions of Services (3.1.3-3.1.4). (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 3.1)

q: Adding Fee plus R together, what Total Cost of Service should be billed to the Client?
n: Total Cost of Service = Fee + R = ₱140,000 + ₱15,000 (reimbursable travel/lodging) = ₱155,000. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1 (Formula: Total Cost of Service = Fee + R))
scenario: A Client engages an Architect to carry out a feasibility study as a Pre-Design Service, compensated under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method. Time logs show the Architect himself put in 40 hours at ₱800/hour, a Consultant contributed 20 hours at ₱1,000/hour, and the Technical Staff logged 60 hours at ₱300/hour. To cover overhead and profit, the firm applies a multiplier of 2.0. Since the project site sits 150 km from the Architect's area of operation, the Consultant and Technical Staff ran up reimbursable travel and lodging costs totaling ₱15,000. On top of that, the Client asked for 8 sets of the feasibility report, more than the standard number of copies ordinarily submitted to the Client.

q: Per Sec. 2.6, what specifically does Architectural Research consist of?
o: Cost estimates from past bid data only
A literature review with no primary data
Primary and secondary research as a basis
Structural computations for the building
n: Sec. 2.6 defines Architectural Research as the conduct of primary and secondary researches and assembled facts used as basis for conclusion. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.6)

q: Per Sec. 2.4, what does Site Selection and Analysis actually entail?
o: Drafting the building permit application
Setting site criteria and helping pick the site
Brokering the site purchase
Preparing the final design for the site
n: Sec. 2.4 defines Site Selection and Analysis as formulating site criteria and assisting the Client in evaluating and analyzing sites to determine the most appropriate one. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.4)

q: Applying Fee = Direct Cost × M with the firm's stated multiplier, what is the Architect's resulting Fee?
n: Fee = Direct Cost x M = ₱70,000 x 2.0 = ₱140,000. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1 (Formula: Fee = Direct Cost x M))
scenario: A Client engages an Architect to carry out a feasibility study as a Pre-Design Service, compensated under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method. Time logs show the Architect himself put in 40 hours at ₱800/hour, a Consultant contributed 20 hours at ₱1,000/hour, and the Technical Staff logged 60 hours at ₱300/hour. To cover overhead and profit, the firm applies a multiplier of 2.0. Since the project site sits 150 km from the Architect's area of operation, the Consultant and Technical Staff ran up reimbursable travel and lodging costs totaling ₱15,000. On top of that, the Client asked for 8 sets of the feasibility report, more than the standard number of copies ordinarily submitted to the Client.

q: Which data-gathering methods does Space Planning (Sec. 2.8) cite?
o: Satellite imagery alone
Interviews, FGDs, surveys and space audits
Financial audits alone
Building code review alone
n: Sec. 2.8 states Space Planning is done through primary data gathering (interviews, consultations, interfaces, FGDs, space planning surveys, space audits) and subsequent analyses such as spatial layouts with stacking concepts. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.8)

q: On what basis do Space Management Studies (Sec. 2.9) analyze space requirements, and what do they yield?
o: Organization and function; yields the space program
The Client's personal taste alone
The site's topography alone
The contractor's work sequence
n: Sec. 2.9 states the analysis is based on organizational structure and functional set-up, pinpointing linkages and interaction of spaces, with the resulting space program serving as basis for the architectural plan/design. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.9)

q: Had the firm instead used the lowest end of the allowable multiplier range (1.5) rather than 2.0, what Fee would have resulted?
n: Fee = Direct Cost x M = ₱70,000 x 1.5 = ₱105,000, since Sec. 4.1 allows the multiplier to range from 1.5 to 2.5. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1 (multiplier range 1.5-2.5))
scenario: A Client engages an Architect to carry out a feasibility study as a Pre-Design Service, compensated under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method. Time logs show the Architect himself put in 40 hours at ₱800/hour, a Consultant contributed 20 hours at ₱1,000/hour, and the Technical Staff logged 60 hours at ₱300/hour. To cover overhead and profit, the firm applies a multiplier of 2.0. Since the project site sits 150 km from the Architect's area of operation, the Consultant and Technical Staff ran up reimbursable travel and lodging costs totaling ₱15,000. On top of that, the Client asked for 8 sets of the feasibility report, more than the standard number of copies ordinarily submitted to the Client.

q: A prospective Client asks an Architect whether it truly matters if the Architect only comes in after a project's basic parameters have already been set by others. Based on Sec. 1.2, how should the Architect respond?
o: Only foreign consultants should come in early
It makes no difference when he comes in
Early involvement benefits the Client most
Early involvement raises his liability
n: Sec. 1.2 states it is most advantageous to the Client to involve the Architect at the earliest stages, since a suitably experienced Architect provides objective project analysis and optimizes building needs versus resources and constraints. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 1.2)

q: Which factors do Site Utilization and Land-Use Studies (Sec. 2.5) analyze?
o: The Client's aesthetic preferences only
The soil's bearing capacity only
Development potential under context and controls
The site's boundaries and title only
n: Sec. 2.5 states the analysis identifies the site's development potentials through proper land utilization, covering the site's context, its surrounding environment, and applicable development controls. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.5)

q: Broadly speaking, why does SPP Doc. 201 insist that the Architect submit a written proposal (Sec. 3.1) before starting Pre-Design Services, rather than simply proceeding on a verbal request?
o: Only written proposals may go to the PRC Board
Every service must be notarized
To settle scope, payment and duties from the start
Verbal agreements are void under the Civil Code
n: Sec. 3.1 requires a proposal stating scope, payment terms, Owner's responsibilities, and other conditions precisely so that the terms of engagement are clear before pre-design work begins, consistent with the document's overall aim of professionalizing the Architect-Client relationship from the earliest stage. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 3.1)

q: A government agency asks its engaged Architect to also produce and coordinate activities that build public acceptance for a proposed project. Under Sec. 2.12 (Promotional Services), what must the Architect keep intact while performing this role?
o: Final control of the project budget
A permit as an advertising agency
Silence toward governing agencies
His status as the Owner's agent
n: Sec. 2.12 states that in acting as agent of the Owner for promotional activities, the Architect must maintain his/her professional status as the representative of the Owner. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.12)

q: To what type of project does Lump Sum or Fixed Fee (Sec. 4.3) apply, and for what reason?
o: Only interior design projects
Only private residential projects, since these are simplest to scope
Government projects, since they involve more paperwork and time-consuming effort
Projects with no defined scope of work
n: Sec. 4.3 states this method may be applied to government projects since they entail more paper work and time-consuming efforts. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.3)

q: Under Sec. 4.1, across what range does the multiplier applied to technical service costs (to cover overhead and profit) fall, and what factors push it toward either end of that range?
o: 1.5 to 2.5, by office, experience and complexity
2.5 to 4.0, by the Client's budget only
No range; negotiated case by case
1.0 to 1.2, fixed for every project
n: Sec. 4.1 (and the Formula section) states the multiplier ranges from 1.5 to 2.5 depending on the office set-up, overhead, experience of the Architect, and complexity of the Project. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1)

q: What does Value Management (Sec. 2.10) aim to achieve?
o: An unimpaired program at minimum cost, where the value-managed plan/design/system still meets the same performance criteria as costlier alternatives
Maximizing the Architect's professional fee
Eliminating the need for a feasibility study
Cutting the program's scope regardless of the impact on performance
n: Sec. 2.10 states the goal of value management is an unimpaired program at minimum cost, with the value-managed result still meeting the same performance criteria as costlier alternatives. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.10)

q: Which set of architectural services does SPP Document 201 govern, and which document does it replace?
o: Design Services; it replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 202
Post-Construction Services; it replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 401
Construction Supervision; it replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 301
Pre-Design Services; it replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 201
n: SPP Document 201, part of the IRR of R.A. No. 9266, covers Pre-Design Services and expressly replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 201. (Source: SPP Document 201, Title/Header)

q: An Architect's proposal to a Client for Pre-Design Services covers the Scope of Work and the fee, but says nothing about what the Owner must furnish or any other conditions. Under Sec. 3.1, what is this proposal missing?
o: A construction timeline, which SPP Doc. 201 requires in every proposal
A statement of the Owner's Responsibilities and Other Conditions of Services
Nothing — the proposal is already complete
The Architect's PRC license number alone
n: Sec. 3.1 requires the proposal to also state the Owner's Responsibilities and Other Conditions of Services, in addition to Scope of Work and Manner of Payment. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 3.1)

q: What does Sec. 4.5 (Mixed Methods of Compensation) say about picking a compensation method for a given project?
o: Only one method may ever apply
More than one method may apply to a project
The Client alone picks the method
Mixed methods are barred
n: Sec. 4.5 states the SPP provides for more than one method of compensation on a project, and each project should be examined to determine the most appropriate and equitable method. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.5)

q: Before both parties settle on the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method, what must the Architect first disclose to the Client?
o: The Architect's income tax return
Personnel rates and the multiplier
Only the total cost estimate
Nothing; disclosure is optional
n: Sec. 4.1 requires the Architect to make known to the Client, at the start of the commission, the rate of professionals/personnel assigned and the multiplier to be applied, before agreeing on this method. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1)

q: According to Sec. 4, on what is the Architect's compensation fundamentally based?
o: The size of the Architect's office
Years since licensure alone
Talent, skill, experience and service level
A fixed government rate
n: Sec. 4 states compensation is based on the Architect's/firm's talents, skill, experience, imagination, and on the type and level of professional services provided. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4)

q: Under Sec. 2.1, at what point does an Architect deliver valuable input through Consultation?
o: Whenever the Client asks for advice or appraisal
Only if the project goes ahead
Only after a full-services agreement
Only during construction
n: Sec. 2.1 states the Architect renders valuable inputs through consultation whether or not the Client pursues the project. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.1)

q: Under Design Brief Preparation (Sec. 2.11), what does the Architect set out, and for what purpose?
o: The project ToR, to bid out architectural services
The as-built survey of a structure
The final construction cost estimate
The Client's financial statements
n: Sec. 2.11 states the Architect prepares the project terms of reference (ToR) — concept, objectives, and other requirements — to bid out architectural services, whether public or private. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.11)

q: What kind of data do Pre-Feasibility Studies (Sec. 2.2) primarily rely on, and toward what end?
o: Validated secondary data, for early decisions
Site survey data, for floor area ratios
As-built data from similar projects
Primary data, to finalize drawings
n: Sec. 2.2 describes Pre-Feasibility Studies as using secondary information gathered and processed to aid the Client's early decision-making and let the Client explore available/readily identifiable directions. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 2.2)

q: Applying the Formula (Direct Cost = AN + CN + TN) from SPP Doc. 201, Sec. 4.1, what is the Direct Cost of this engagement?
n: AN = 40 hrs x ₱800 = ₱32,000; CN = 20 hrs x ₱1,000 = ₱20,000; TN = 60 hrs x ₱300 = ₱18,000. Direct Cost = 32,000 + 20,000 + 18,000 = ₱70,000. (Source: SPP Document 201, Sec. 4.1 (Formula: Direct Cost = AN + CN + TN))
